title: The Budha Dal today
hook: the Nihang army traces itself to the elders' Dal of this century

segments.voice: Yesterday, remembering without hatred: the Ardas names the martyrs, not the enemies, and asks the good of all. Your line was courage, not revenge. Where did you turn an old story toward who stood? Day eight hundred seventy-eight.

Deep blue robes. A turban wound high, almost a tower, ringed with steel circles and small blades. A spear in hand, a horse nearby, and a voice calling out the Khalsa's victory cry. If you've seen photographs from the festival of Hola Mohalla at Anandpur, you may have seen them: the Nihangs. They can look like figures stepped out of an old painting. They aren't a reenactment. They say they are the same army that rode through the century you've been hearing about, still riding. Today: the Budha Dal today.
screen: `BLUE ROBES, A TOWERING TURBAN.` → `HOLA MOHALLA AT ANANDPUR.` → `THE SAME ARMY, STILL RIDING.`

segments.voice: Go back a few weeks on this path. The Khalsa organized its riders into two bodies: the Budha Dal, the army of the elders, and the Taruna Dal, the army of the young. Budha means old. The elders' Dal kept the camps, guarded the shrines, held the memory. That's where today starts. The Nihang groups of today trace themselves to that body. One of them still carries the name Budha Dal and has its own jathedar, its own leader, and its own camps that move from place to place. In their telling, the line was never broken. The second thing is what they keep. Tradition says the Nihangs hold on to ways of the old riders that ordinary life elsewhere has left behind: the blue dress, the high turban with its weapons, life in moving camps, care for horses, the martial art called gatka, and a coded, joking way of speaking that belongs to the camps. To spend time with them is to see the hard century as a practice, not a chapter. The third thing is honest complexity. There's more than one Nihang Dal today, and they don't all agree, with each other or with other Sikhs, about every practice. Sikhs hold a range of views about them. What's clear is the claim they make: that the riders of the hard century didn't only leave descendants and stories. They left an army that still keeps its camp. The old army lives.
screen: `BUDHA DAL: THE ARMY OF THE ELDERS.` · `NIHANGS TRACE THEMSELVES TO IT.` · `BLUE DRESS, GATKA, MOVING CAMPS.` · `MORE THAN ONE DAL, MORE THAN ONE VIEW.` · then, large: `THE OLD ARMY LIVES.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with something living. Settle, and breathe. Bring up a tradition you've seen kept alive by real people: a recipe your grandmother still makes the old way, a song only sung at weddings, a craft somebody in your town still does by hand. Picture the person keeping it. Notice how much effort it takes, and how easily it could have stopped with them. Let yourself be a little grateful that it didn't. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Nihang. The order of Sikh warriors who say they are the elders' army of the hard century still riding: blue robes, high turbans, moving camps. Today's word.
Your line: the old army lives. Today, notice one old way that someone near you still keeps, and ask them about it. Day eight hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Nihang Sikhs live in Dals with their own leaders and moving camps, wear blue with high turbans, keep horses and practice gatka, and gather for Hola Mohalla at Anandpur.

fork.setup: you're a rider in the elders' Dal. the hard century ends, the land is settled, and the war is over. what happens to your Dal?
options: it disbands, and everyone goes home to farm.
it keeps its camp, its dress and its ways, and carries them on.
it becomes a regular government army.
fork.reveal: the Nihangs of the Budha Dal say their camp never broke up: they still keep the dress, the horses and the moving camps of the old riders.

original.note: Gurmukhi for Nihang, the name of the Sikh order that keeps the old Dals.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Budha Dal is a chapter in a history book.
what it means: Nihang Sikhs today trace themselves to the elders' army and keep its dress, horses and moving camps.

what a scholar hears: one Nihang body still carries the name Budha Dal with its own jathedar, and the Nihangs are a living link to the practice of the hard century, though several Dals exist and views about them vary.

notes: Nihang continuity with the eighteenth-century Budha Dal is presented as the Nihangs' own claim; confirm framing.
Practices listed (blue dress, high dumalla with weapons, moving camps, horses, gatka, coded camp speech 'Nihang bole'): confirm and adjust.
No dates or numbers in the voice; the period is called 'the hard century' throughout.
Hola Mohalla at Anandpur as the best-known public gathering of Nihangs: confirm.
The note that several Dals exist and that Sikhs hold a range of views about them should be checked for fairness.
